source.title: PolyLM: An Open Source Polyglot Large Language Model
source.authors: Xiangpeng Wei; Hao-Ran Wei; Huan Lin; Tianhao Li; Pei Zhang; Xingzhang Ren; Mei Li; Yu Wan; Zhiwei Cao; Binbin Xie; Tianxiang Hu; Shangjie Li; Binyuan Hui; Yu Bowen; Dayiheng Liu; Baosong Yang; Fei Huang; Jun Xie

record.tranche_reason: Compares downstream multilingual task performance at two model sizes, a different measure from held-out pretraining loss and fitted scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling-law work but reports no held-out loss sweeps, power-law fits, small-run extrapolations, or compute-optimal allocation tests. Its own comparison of 1.7B and 13B models on downstream multilingual tasks bears on V6; the individual task values are shown in Figure 13 without numeric values in the text.
record.test_reason: Section 6.3 compares PolyLM-1.7B and 13B, both trained on the same 638B tokens, on multilingual downstream tasks in a one-shot setting. That bears weakly on V6 in a new, multilingual setting. It is only two sizes, with no loss sweep or fit, so it shows improvement with scale but cannot show predictability. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report that 13B significantly outperforms 1.7B on all compared multilingual tasks. They speculate that multilingual tasks depend more on model capacity, and name refining a multilingual scaling law as a future goal.
record.recipe_differences: Compares two model sizes using multilingual downstream-task performance, rather than fitting power laws to held-out pretraining loss or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.problems: Only two model sizes are compared for the scaling-related result; the supplied text gives no numeric values or uncertainty for Figure 13 and reports no scaling-law fit.

untested.parts: Whether downstream gains follow a predictable curve in scale, any relation to pretraining loss, and sizes beyond two points.
All: no held-out loss sweep across sizes or tokens.
All: both sizes use the same token count.

record.verdict_notes: This is mainly a model-release report; the scaling comparison is a brief analysis. Figures 2-3 show training-loss curves for stability only, not scaling. Figure 13 values are absent from the extracted text, so the size of the gain cannot be checked.

versions.untested_parts: Whether downstream performance follows a predictable scaling curve, its relationship to pretraining loss, and performance at additional model sizes.

rows.subject: POLYLM-13B vs POLYLM-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared model sizes on multilingual downstream tasks.
rows.measure: Performance across the compared multilingual tasks
rows.value: POLYLM-13B significantly outperforms POLYLM-1.7B across all compared multilingual tasks.
rows.note: The paper reports this as an aggregate across the compared tasks; Figure 13 does not provide numeric values in the supplied text.
rows.check: The row is linked correctly. The state holds only for the direction of improvement: two sizes cannot show a predictable trend. The two models also differ in peak learning rate (1e-4 vs 6e-5) and batch size (512 vs 2048), not just size. Figure 13 values are not readable in the text, so no effect size is available.

relationships.condition: PolyLM 1.7B vs 13B, same 638B-token data, one-shot multilingual NLU and MT tasks
relationships.reason: The authors state the 13B model significantly outperforms the 1.7B model on all compared tasks (r1). This supports direction only, not predictability, from two points with confounded hyperparameters.
relationships.display_finding: The 13B model significantly outperformed 1.7B on every compared task, although the two-size comparison confounded hyperparameters and did not establish predictability.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: POLYLM models at 1.7B and 13B on the compared multilingual tasks
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the larger model significantly outperforms the smaller one across all compared tasks (r1); this supports a scale-related improvement in this tested comparison, not a predictive scaling law.
